description: Europium is a silvery-white metal of the lanthanide series with atomic number 63 and symbol Eu. It is the most chemically reactive, least dense, and softest of the lanthanides, soft enough to be cut with a knife. It reacts readily with air to form a dark oxide coating and was discovered in 1896, then named after the continent of Europe in 1901.
uses: Most applications of europium exploit the phosphorescence of europium compounds. Divalent europium in small amounts is the activator of the bright blue fluorescence of some samples of the mineral fluorite. In astrophysics, the signature of europium in stellar spectra can be used to classify stars and inform theories of stellar formation.
characteristics: Europium is a ductile metal with hardness similar to that of lead that crystallizes in a body-centered cubic lattice. It rapidly oxidizes in air and has reactivity with water comparable to that of calcium, igniting at 150 to 180 °C. Although usually trivalent, europium readily forms divalent compounds with an electron configuration of 4f7, which is unusual among lanthanides.
